data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Navigation often relies on inductive habits (sun rises in east), whereas Popper forbids this.","A cliff is a permanent physical feature; a falsified theory might be revised or contextualized."],"overturn_conditions":["If the terrain changes unpredictably such that past cliffs become safe and safe paths become cliffs instantly, the elimination strategy fails completely.","If the agent secretly believes the safe path 'probably' won't collapse, they have smuggled induction back in."],"shared_structure":["Agent must choose a path despite lacking a map of the future.","Choice is based on eliminating paths known to lead to cliffs (falsification).","Surviving paths are not 'probable' to be safe, just 'not known' to be deadly."],"source_memory_refs":["nav_map_crossing"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a navigator chooses the un-fallen path not because it 'will' hold, but because others 'did' fall, scientists choose corroborated theories to avoid known errors.","The rationality of the crossing lies in the elimination of danger, not the prediction of safety."]},"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' that minimizes the risk of acting on known falsehoods, rather than maximizing the probability of future success; however, accepting this defense costs the agent any rational assurance that the future will resemble the past, reducing scientific action to a gamble where the only 'rationality' lies in having critically eliminated the worst available options.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature to be effective, the distinction collapses into hidden induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) cannot be formally defined without inductive assumptions, the risk-minimization argument lacks a logical foundation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory inherently demands a belief in its future reliability, then claiming 'no probability' is merely semantic evasion.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'criticism' (which relies on deduction). It posits that while corroboration reports only past performance, choosing the best-corroborated theory is a methodological rule to avoid theories already proven false or inferior in specific tests. This transforms the choice from an inductive prediction ('A will work because it did') to a risk-management strategy ('A is the least-wrong known option, so if we must act, we act on A').","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
